title: Update: what happened after you stress-tested my 4h trend bot (Binance futures, built with Claude)
author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
selftext:
A few days ago I posted my bot here and some of you asked for harder tests: point-in-time universe with delisted coins, random baskets, placebo entries, t-stats per month. I ran all of them. Here's the honest result.



**What the tests said**

\- Point-in-time universe (top 45 by volume each month, incl. delisted): the edge survives but it's smaller, about +2 to +4 cents per $12.5 trade after fees and slippage.

\- t-stat per month: 1.6–1.8. So: promising, NOT proven.

\- Random entries with the same stops do NOT beat buy-and-hold. The entry signal is what carries the edge (bot minus random: t 2.7).

\- The edge is almost all SHORT, and it lives in altcoin bear regimes. LONG was close to noise, so it now trades smaller and only when BTC is above its 4h EMA 200.

\- The edge comes in cycles (strong 2022, weak 2023-24, back in 2025). Re-tuning the exits every year did not help, which suggests the exits aren't overfit.



**What I changed (all decided with rules written BEFORE seeing results)**

\- Second batch of shorts (positions 9-16 per side) only when BTC is below its 4h EMA 200.

\- Trailing stop per side: LONG 4 ATR, SHORT 3 ATR.

\- Partial take-profit: half at +3.5 ATR.

\- Discarded after testing: correlation caps, pullback entries, pyramiding, volatility sizing (twice), equity-curve filter, other timeframes, 15m, Binance listing announcements (the move is over in under a minute).



**Live so far (trend-only since Nov 5, \~$250 beta account I'm OK losing)**

\- 3 closed trend trades: +1.29 USD. 6 shorts open, all with stops already in profit.

\- That's nothing statistically. My bar is 300 live trades, and I built a "traffic light" from the backtest: the normal range of cumulative results for N trades. Grey until 25 trades, then green/yellow/red. Red = review, not panic-switch-off.



**Ops stuff I added because of your comments**

\- Every stop lives on Binance from the first second, plus a trailing backup.

\- Order book measured before each market exit. One stop already slipped 0.33% vs the 0.055% I assume in backtests, so I'm logging until \~50 stops before judging.

\- External heartbeat, daily backup, a 168-check regression test suite before every install.



**Questions for you**

1. With a small live sample, how do you decide live is "consistent with the backtest" without fooling yourself?

2. Anyone measured stop slippage on Binance alts vs order book depth? Is 0.055% realistic?



Thanks to everyone who pushed back last time. It made the bot more honest, and smaller in expectations. I'll post again at 100 live trades, good or bad.

Over the last weeks I’ve tested 60+ strategies and filters (including 18 rules taken from trading books) across 56 research labs, about 250 parameter variants in total, on a 6-year backtest with 677 Binance perpetuals including delisted coins. Only one thing kept an edge: 4h trend-following. Every install also has to pass 168 automated checks.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
The traffic light idea is really nice, and deciding that red means review, not switch off, before going live is the hard part most people skip.

One thing on question 1: I'd rebuild that band with the slippage you're actually seeing on stops, not the 0.055%. Otherwise the band itself is too optimistic, and live will drift into yellow because of costs, not because the signal stopped working. Hard to tell those two apart later.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Great point, thanks. You're right: if the band assumes 0.055% and live stops slip more, the light drifts yellow for cost reasons and I'd misread it as the signal decaying.



I only have one measured live stop so far (0.33%), so instead of rebuilding on one data point I ran the sensitivity. Extra slippage is roughly a fixed cost per trade, so it shifts the whole band down (assumed 90% of exits are market stops, $12.5 per trade):



Median cumulative after 300 trades: +35.7 at 0.055% · +32.5 at 0.15% · +26.4 at 0.33%

Yellow line at 300 trades: +6.9 · +3.7 · -2.4



So at 0.15% it barely matters. At 0.33% on every stop the expected result drops \~26% (still positive), and the band would be clearly optimistic past \~100 trades. Below \~50 trades the extra cost (\~$1.5) is small next to normal variance, so it won't flip the color early.



Plan: I'm already logging order book depth and actual fill vs stop price on every stop. At \~50 live stops I'll rebuild the band with the measured slippage, and the light will show the result before and after slippage, so I can tell costs from signal.



Good catch, this is exactly the kind of thing that would have fooled me later.

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: Makes sense to wait for 50 instead of rebuilding on one stop. Might be worth logging ATR or some volatility number next to each fill too, since stops tend to slip the most exactly when a lot of them fire at once.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Good one. Right now each fill logs spread, depth within 0.5%, book imbalance and actual slippage, but nothing about volatility or clustering. And I've seen the clustering firsthand: an earlier version had 20 stops fire in 17 minutes during one dump.



Adding to the next version (logging only, no trading changes):

\- ATR % of the coin at the fill

\- 1h move of the coin and of BTC

\- how many of the bot's own stops filled within ±5 min



Then at \~50 stops I can split slippage into clustered vs isolated and by volatility tercile, instead of one average that hides the cascade days. Thanks!

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Early on, I'd compare the parts of each trade that you can measure now, like fill price against signal price, fees, and average win against average loss, instead of waiting for the total P&L to settle. Those show whether live behaves like the backtest long before 300 trades. On slippage, one fixed number is risky for stops, because they tend to fire when the book is thinnest and the misses are bigger than average. The edge you describe is only a few tenths of a percent per trade, so a 0.33% stop slip is about the size of the whole edge. I'd rerun the backtest with stops filled at a worse, fat-tailed slippage and see if it still holds up. Writing down what counts as red before the live sample grows is a good call too.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Really useful, thanks. I ran it.



First, a correction to my own post: the "+2 to +4 cents per $12.5 trade" was from the original rule set. With the current rules the unbiased 6-year backtest is \~12.9 cents per trade, and the recent 3 years on my coin list \~8.2 cents. So 0.33% is a big bite, but not the whole edge.



Then I reran the same trades with fat-tailed stop slippage instead of a fixed 0.055%. Mostly small, sometimes large, rarely huge, and x2 / x3 when 5+ / 10+ of the bot's stops fire in the same 4h candle. 200 draws per scenario:



\- Moderate (avg \~0.13%): 12.9 -> 11.7 cents/trade (6y unbiased), 8.2 -> 7.0 (recent)

\- Hard (avg \~0.25%, tail to 2%): 12.9 -> 10.5, 8.2 -> 5.7



Two things I didn't expect: 98% of exits are stops (I'd assumed 90%), and 18% of stops fire in clusters of 5+ in the same candle. So you were right that clustering is common.



The edge survives even the hard case (rule written before running it), but the band gets less forgiving: the yellow line at 300 trades goes from +6.9 to -0.5. Caveat: same trades in every draw, so this measures expected cost, not trade luck.



And I'll add your "compare the parts" idea: avg win, avg loss, win rate, entry and stop slippage, each against its backtest value. That gives a read long before 300 trades.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Rerunning it and correcting your own number is the kind of check that makes the bot's numbers worth trusting. The cluster finding matters most to me, because stops firing together means your losses are correlated. That's a portfolio risk, so a cap on how many shorts can be open at once, or on total open risk, may matter more than the per-trade slippage figure. The live log should show whether fills on those cluster candles are worse than on single stops, which would justify an even harsher assumption for them.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Agreed, clustered stops mean it's closer to one big bet than many small ones. I tested caps on that side earlier:



\- A correlation cap (limiting coins that move together) didn't pass. In the backtest it cut profit more than it cut drawdown.

\- Going the other way, more slots, actually improved results. That's why there's a second batch of shorts, but only when BTC is below its 4h EMA 200.

\- Current limits: 8 per side (+8 shorts in a BTC downtrend), max 2x total exposure, a 5% daily loss brake, and a cascade brake if many stops fire in a short window.



So the cap is there, just looser than you'd maybe expect, because the edge lives in exactly those correlated alt dumps.



On the fills: yes, next version logs how many of the bot's stops filled within ±5 min, plus ATR and the 1h move of the coin and BTC. If cluster fills turn out worse, I'll price them harsher in the band. Already did x2 / x3 in the sim as a guess.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body: With only three closed trades, I'd focus on whether the live signals and fills match what the backtest would have done, not the P&L yet. That 0.33% stop slippage is worth tracking separately. Even a good signal won't save an edge if the execution assumptions are too optimistic.
